History books love romantic tales, like the one where Lee Iacocca, father of the Mustang, was responsible for giving birth to a whole new category of vehicles: pony cars. Sure, he was behind the creation of the most popular such vehicle, but the pony car concept was in the brewing stage years before the first-gen Mustang Mk1. While not strictly pony cars, these concepts and production sporty coupés already flirted with the concept of an enthusiast-grade compact car.

Of course, we don't mean to diminish Iacocca's genius. Yes, he didn't invent the wheel, but he definitely read the room better than his counterparts. In fact, some of the cars featured in this piece influenced him to create the special team of engineers that worked on the Mustang. From early Ford-based compact sports cars like the Budd XT-Bird Concept and Ford Falcon Futura Sport to rear-engine fun machines like the Chevrolet Corvair Monza Turbo, these pre-Mustang models warmed the public to the pony car idea.

If you know anything about internal combustion, you'll know that spark plugs are key to performance and efficiency. But there are two main types of spark plugs on offer today: iridium and platinum, and the choice of spark plug can make a difference on how your car engine performs. That said, it's more nuanced than simply choosing one over the other, and it greatly depends on the application. First, the basics. Spark plugs in a gasoline engine play a key role because, without them, the gas-air mixture would not combust, and simply put, you'd go nowhere.

But even though they're a cornerstone of any gas engine — virtually as old as the invention itself — the tech behind them continues to develop. In the old days, spark plugs were made of copper. Copper is no longer used on modern cars because it wears out relatively quickly inside a cylinder of exploding gas that can routinely exceed 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit in normal operation. So, which type of spark plug is better? To answer that, we need to discuss which is most cost-effective for your situation and whether can you mix and match the two.

It feels like trucks get bigger and bigger every year. The differences between modern trucks and their predecessors are abundantly clear when you look at something like a Ford F-150 from the 1970s alongside a modern version: cabs are getting longer, beds are getting shorter, and footprints keep expanding. This is, in part, the result of George W. Bush-era revisions to the Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, which linked each truck's fuel-economy target to its footprint, holding bigger trucks to lower mpg targets.

While some automakers have abandoned the compact and midsize truck segments, the ones still going strong are pretty impressive. In particular, the Ford Maverick is nearly the perfect truck , even with its un-trucklike unibody design. And if its excellent hybrid fuel efficiency, spiffy handling, user-friendly tech, and agreeable ride don't sell it for you, then maybe some of its hidden features will.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) is the result of years of negotiations on permitting reform. The product is a bill that combines critically important transmission and grid reforms with significant and concerning changes to federal environmental laws, permitting standards, and judicial remedies.

The transmission provisions in the bill would produce substantial and durable benefits, updating an aging power grid by allowing new investments. These reforms, which NRDC has long supported, are an essential component of accelerating the electrification and decarbonization of the power sector and achieving greenhouse gas reduction targets. On their own, these changes are much needed and overdue; they would also help any future clean energy incentives and standards succeed in cutting emissions. But transmission is an enabling technology rather than a substitute for policies that directly drive clean energy investment and reduce pollution.

You get them. I get them. We all get them. AI robocalls are a nightmare scourge on society that are driving everybody to the brink of their sanity. Usually, they're from some sort of money-lending organization. Still, one Massachusetts man says he keeps receiving pre-recorded phone calls from Cambridge Honda asking him whether he was interested in selling them his car. Now, he's seeking class-action status against the dealership, alleging that it violated the Telephone Consumer Protection Act.

Plaintiff Jonathan Kamens has never been a customer at Cambridge Honda , and his cell phone number is on the National Do Not Call Registry, according to Automotive News . The complaint alleges that an AI-generated caller with a "robotic and artificial voice" addresses Kamens by the wrong name, "Timothy," and then says, "Roger from Cambridge Honda. Reaching out because you're one of our customers, and your car happens to be on a list of models we are looking to buy. If you're open to an instant cash offer on your car, give me a call at (351) 300-0683. Thanks." Kamens added that he received subsequent texts from "Roger" inviting him to sell his vehicle — something he really has no interest in doing.

Despite what its name suggests, Tesla's FSD system is only a Level 2 system. This means it is not technically a hands-off, eyes-off, or mind-off system, where the driver can completely relax while behind the wheel. As a result, Turo is encouraging users to read Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised) safety documentation before booking a ride. That's smart on Turo's part, but we can't help but think very few users will bother, and they'll probably end up booking Teslas they think are fully autonomous, only to find out they're not. Henrik Fisker probably had no idea how fitting the name Karma would be when he launched the plug-in hybrid sedan in 2011 under his eponymous startup. In Hinduism, karma is intrinsically linked to reincarnation, the karma accumulated in one life affecting the conditions of the next life. Fisker’s venture wound up failing in 2014, but after Wanxiang Group, a Chinese automotive parts conglomerate, bought the assets, the car was reborn as the Karma Revero. The Revero has been built since 2016 and has undergone several updates, but the tiny California-based company has struggled to gain a foothold.

Now Karma Automotive is seeking to reinvent itself, and it will start by giving the plug-in hybrid sedan yet another reincarnation. Marques McCammon—previously of DaimlerChrysler, Roush, Saleen, and engineering firm Ricardo—joined as president of the company in 2023, and the 2027 Gyesera is the first product launched under his guidance. While it retains similarities to the sedans that preceded it, a lightly updated powertrain and a fresh design language aim to set the brand up for a brighter future. Driving a pre-production version of the Gyesera in and around Las Vegas, we discovered a car that feels special and provides enticing powertrain flexibility but that is still bound by some of the same flaws as its predecessors.

Its bright Canary Yellow paint was an original color for this sporty take on the classic small truck, not a flashy add-on. Motors FB1-4001A motor makes somewhere between 18 and 30 horsepower, a significant downgrade from the original 140 or so from the V6. Compact crossover sales account for a massive share of new car sales each year behind only the full-size pickup segment, with heavyweights like the Honda CR-V, Toyota RAV4 , Tesla Model Y , and Nissan Rogue all making the list of the top 10 best-selling cars in the U.S. through Q3 of this year.
